newsitem.title: USA: Ronald Goldman's sister speaks out after verdict.
newsitem.headline: Ronald Goldman's sister speaks out after verdict.

text.p: Making her first public appearance since O.J. Simpson was found responsible for her brother's death, Kim Goldman said on Thursday the civil jury's verdict gave her back "some faith" in the judicial process.
"I think the system worked," said Goldman, who spoke out bitterly after a criminal jury cleared the former football star of double murder charges in 1995.

Goldman, a familiar sight at Simpson's civil and criminal trials, appeared in New York to accept a donation from No Excuses sportswear company for Safe Streets Alliance. Her father is a spokesman for the criminal justice reform group.
She burst into tears as she tried to explain how she would like her older brother, Ron Goldman, to be remembered.
"My brother didn't run. He fought for his life. He fought for Nicole. That's what he did all his life," she said before sobs overtook her.
She also described how her family "hugged, cried and made a toast to my brother" after hearing the jury's decision.
She said they do not fear any efforts by Simpson to appeal Tuesday's civil verdict which held him responsible for the June 12, 1994 murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and Goldman.
"You can't hit our family any harder than we have been hit," she said.

Asked what she planned to do next, Goldman answered, "Breathe." She also said that she would like to finish her college degree. She was studying psychology in San Francsico and took a leave of absence when her brother was killed. But she added, "It'll never be over. This is only one chapter."

Fred Goldman announced last fall that he would become the public affairs director for Safe Streets, a Washington-based group that campaigns for tougher laws for sex offenders, jury reform and mandatory sentencing and against parole for hard-core criminals.

A spokesman for Safe Streets, Mark Gilman, defended its decision to accept the donation from No Excuses. The sportswear company has used such controversial spokeswomen as Donna Rice, who was caught in a liaison with 1988 presidential hopeful Gary Hart, and Marla Maples, linked to developer Donald Trump while he was still married to his first wife.
Gilman said No Excuses had since changed ownership and its image.

No Excuses gave $50,000 in 1994 to Paula Jones, who has accused President Bill Clinton of sexual harassment, to promote its sportswear. She agreed to give half of the money away, but an Arkansas shelter for battered women turned it down for fear it would alienate other donors.
No Excuses also made a donation to Nicole Brown Simpson's sister, Denise Brown, to launch an anti-domestic violence group.
